query: Why did hardware incidents spike in the anomaly window?

per_column.name: weekly_hardware_count
per_column.rationale: The weekly count of hardware incidents is essentially the operationalized outcome itself (the spike is defined on this series), not a distinct treatment or confounder.

per_column.name: weekly_hardware_pct
per_column.rationale: Hardware share of incidents per week is another restatement of the outcome magnitude, not a candidate cause or common cause of a treatment.

per_column.name: hw_rolling_avg_prior4w
per_column.rationale: A prior-4-week baseline of hardware volume; it is a lagged version of the outcome used to define the spike ratio, functioning as a normalization baseline rather than a treatment or a common cause of any treatment.

per_column.name: hw_spike_ratio
per_column.rationale: Ratio of current to baseline hardware volume; this is the quantitative definition of the spike (the outcome), not an external cause.

per_column.name: in_anomaly_window
per_column.rationale: A time-window flag copied directly from the query ('the anomaly window'). It marks WHEN the outcome occurred but supplies no candidate cause; it is an indicator of the outcome period, not a treatment or confounder.

judge.rationale: The added columns are all descriptive re-expressions of the outcome itself: weekly counts, percentages, a prior-window baseline, the spike ratio, and a flag for the anomaly window taken verbatim from the query. None of them names a candidate CAUSE of the hardware spike (e.g., a specific deployment, vendor, change request, config update, patch, hardware model, load event). There is therefore no treatment, and consequently no confounders (variables that jointly cause a treatment and the outcome). The operator quantified and localized the spike but never set up any causal estimation, so the causal-attribution claim fails entirely.
